title: Locality-aware fidelity lab - rough PRD & experiments
content:
Brain dump / scratchpad for a feature-ish idea: locality-aware fidelity lanes (name will change).

Goal: reduce end-to-end latency and token-cost for regionally clustered traffic while preserving perceived quality for users whose context/history is locally stable. Kind of a hybrid of routing + cache affinity + fidelity tiering.

Why: noticed repeated tail latency spikes for EU customers when requests hit cross-region KV cache misses or cold model shards. Some customers can tolerate lower-fidelity completions for non-critical flows (autosuggest, search summarization) in exchange for much lower latency/cost.

Hypothesis: if we make routing decisions that consider (1) request locality (client region + inferred affinity to previous session storage), (2) workload criticality (endpoint tag), and (3) cached KV hit probability, we can reduce p95 by 20-40% for prioritized regional flows and cut token-cost by 10-25% overall without measurable drop in quality on targeted eval sets.

Key concepts (quick):
- Locality signal: region header + session-store-geo-tag + latency-from-edge pings.
- Fidelity lanes: HIGH / STANDARD / ECONOMY. Each lane maps to model variant + quantization profile + batching policy.
- Cache affinity: sticky routing to the node/region where a user's KV/prefix cache is warm. TTL-based affinity with soft fallback.
- Warmup prefetchers: for flows with high reuse, prefetch KV cache into regional nodes during low load.
- Graceful degrade: if local capacity not available, fall back to cross-region with exponential backoff and hint-based partial response (e.g., send placeholder + follow-up).

User stories (rough):
- As an internal product engineer, I want app endpoints to advertise whether a flow is latency-first or quality-first so routing can pick ECONOMY vs HIGH.
- As an ML infra engineer, I want a simple policy DSL to encode rules (region match, session affinity threshold, endpoint-criticality) so we can iterate without infra changes.
- As an SRE, I want observability per-lane (cost/token, p50/p95/p99, cache-hit-rate) so we can monitor regressions and set alerts.

Metrics to track:
- latency p50/p95/p99 by lane and region
- KV cache local hit rate (per-customer and aggregated)
- tokens-per-request and cost delta by lane
- eval quality metrics on held prompt sets (ROUGE/EM/semantic-simscore) per lane
- fallback rate (how often local lane falls back to remote)

Experiment plan (MVP-ish):
1) Instrument: gather baseline for two pilot regions (eu-west, us-west) on 2 endpoints: "suggest" (latency-sensitive) and "compose" (quality-sensitive). 1 week of baseline metrics.
2) Policy shim: create lightweight routing shim in front of runtime that can route to: same-region STANDARD model, same-region ECONOMY model (aggressive quant), other-region HIGH model. Default is current behavior.
3) KV affinity: implement soft-sticky cookie that hints preferred region; measure local cache hit improvements.
4) A/B: route 20% of traffic for a subset of customers through policies (priority: small-mid SaaS customers). Run 2-week A/B comparing latency and quality.
5) Evaluate: if p95 improves >20% for suggest and quality delta <2% for compose, expand.

Implementation notes / low-level thoughts:
- Need API surface for endpoint developers to mark endpoint-criticality (maybe a header: x-rw-fidelity: high|std|eco). Also allow per-customer override via console.
- Routing shim should be policy-driven, not hard-coded; store policies in a small config DB (Redis) and push to edge agents.
- ECONOMY model variants can be prebuilt quantized checkpoints with narrower context lengths and prefix-aggregation off. Feels like we need a few pre-made profiles.
- Consider cost accounting: charge tokens differently for ECO vs HIGH? or show cost-reduction insights in console instead.

Open questions / risks:
- Quality regressions are hard to measure; need targeted eval suites that mirror real customer prompts. Who owns these? (ask Eval team)
- Privacy/compliance: caching session prefixes regionally — some customers require data residency; must map to Private/Dedicated policies.
- Sticky affinity may cause uneven load distribution; need cooldown and rebalancing logic.
- Will customers accept differing behavior per-region? need transparency and opt-outs.

Rollout milestones (very rough):
- Week 0-2: baseline data and feature spec; confirm pilot customers
- Week 3-4: routing shim + policy DSL + console toggle prototype (internal only)
- Week 5-6: deploy ECONOMY model variants to pilot region nodes; KV affinity cookie; start A/B
- Week 7-8: evaluate results, iterate on policy thresholds; prepare postmortem and docs

Short TODOs (for me):
- Draft short note for Eval team: need two prompt-sets (suggestion flow + long compose) across 10 customers — ask Maya to sync.
- Create Jira INF-4213 prototype ticket (placeholder already linked).
- Sketch policy DSL examples (if region==eu-west && session-affinity>0.6 -> prefer local-economy unless endpoint==compose).
- Ping Console PM about showing per-lane cost estimates in route settings.

Notes-to-self / heuristics:
- Start conservative: big wins for suggest endpoint are cheap and lower-risk.
- Keep HIGH lane behavior identical to current baseline to avoid regressions.
- Use synthetic warmup (replay recent requests) during low-traffic windows to prime local caches.

Draft policy examples (brain dump):
- policyA: {match: region==client.region && endpoint in [suggest] && sessionAffinity>0.4 -> route: region-economy}
- policyB: {match: customerTier==enterprise -> always route: high}
- policyC: {match: fallbackCount>2 -> route: cross-region-high-with-warn}

Questions for next sync:
- Who on Eval can own building the small prompt sets? (Maya?)
- What's an acceptable quality delta threshold for compose? 1-2%?
- Can Console expose per-route weighting quickly or do we need a flag?

Random thoughts: could extend to locality-aware embeddings cache for retrieval-heavy apps; same affinity logic but for vector shards. Might be a separate epics.

End — will refine into a tidy PRD if reactions look positive. For now this is a working scratchpad; keep messy.
